digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-04
digests.theme: Today is a control logic versus hardware theater day. The strongest preserve-worthy paper is the bioRxiv preprint Passive neuromodulation: an energy-driven mechanism for closed-loop suppression of epileptic seizures, because it states a clean intervention idea instead of treating stimulation as magic: if seizure dynamics can be damped by draining energy from the circuit, then responsive control may not need to look like conventional pulse-train stimulation at all. The most interesting translational hardware paper is Remote Magnetomechanical Neuromodulation Uncovers Therapeutic Mechanisms for Alleviating Parkinsonian Symptoms in Freely Moving Mice, which is flashy but not empty. The most useful targeting and network infrastructure paper is A human subcortical connectome at 400 μm resolution, because serious neuromodulation still lives or dies on whether the field can resolve the subcortical pathways it keeps pretending to target.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Passive neuromodulation: an energy-driven mechanism for closed-loop suppression of epileptic seizures. This is not a clinical paper and it does not pretend to be. Its claim is narrower and more interesting: using two seizure models, the authors argue that an analog feedback element can passively drain energy from an epileptic circuit and suppress seizure initiation or spread without the usual active stimulation logic. They report efficacy in both a detailed dentate-gyrus network model and the Epileptor neural mass model, and they also test a responsive version that turns on for brief windows after seizure detection. The reason to keep this is not that it is ready for patients. The reason is that it sharpens a neglected control idea: some pathological dynamics may be better handled by damping than by repeated forcing. That is a better mechanistic frame than a lot of decorative closed-loop rhetoric.

The second paper worth preserving is Remote Magnetomechanical Neuromodulation Uncovers Therapeutic Mechanisms for Alleviating Parkinsonian Symptoms in Freely Moving Mice. This one has obvious hardware-hype risk, but it is more substantial than the phrase minimally-invasive DBS without chronically implanted hardware would suggest. The core design uses magnetite nanodiscs that generate local torque under low-frequency alternating magnetic fields, aiming to recruit endogenous mechanosensory pathways rather than electrodes or optogenetics. The paper reports in vitro and ex vivo calcium-imaging evidence, remote control of motor behavior in wild-type mice, and improved motor function in a severe hemiparkinsonian mouse model when targeting the subthalamic nucleus. That is interesting translational engineering, but it is still preclinical, and the jump from mechanosensory torque in mice to clinically meaningful human deep-brain control remains enormous.

The third preserve-worthy paper is A human subcortical connectome at 400 μm resolution. This is not a stimulation study, but it may matter more than many nominal stimulation papers because it targets a real bottleneck: the subcortical pathways behind deep brain stimulation and lesion effects are hard to resolve with ordinary diffusion MRI, so the field leans on synthetic or overly smoothed atlases. This paper uses ultra-high-resolution ex vivo diffusion MRI on the Connectome 2.0 scanner to reconstruct basal-ganglia-thalamocortical pathways and then align the resulting atlas to reported deep brain stimulation hotspots and side-effect zones. It should not be mistaken for patient-ready individualized targeting, but it is exactly the kind of anatomical infrastructure that can make future targeting claims less hand-wavy.

A fourth paper that stayed in scope but below the preservation threshold is Precision phase targeting of event-related oscillations using real-time closed-loop TMS-EEG. It is useful methods work. The strongest part is that it avoids prediction-heavy phase targeting and instead directly detects phase in real time, improving trigger probability and phase precision for event-related theta in navigation tasks. But the accessible evidence here is validation without active TMS delivery, so for now it is better treated as a promising platform paper than as a direct intervention result.
digests.takeaway: Today’s honest pattern is that the strongest ideas were not the loudest hardware claims. The best paper is the seizure-control preprint because it makes the intervention logic more explicit: some pathological brain dynamics may be better damped than driven. The magnetomechanical Parkinson paper is worth keeping because it is a real preclinical modality paper, not pure branding, but it still lives far from human therapeutic proof. The subcortical connectome paper is valuable because targeting cannot improve if the anatomy stays blurry. And the phase-targeting TMS paper is a good reminder that better timing infrastructure is useful, but not every precision method deserves immediate preserve status as an intervention result.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-03
digests.theme: Today is a deep-target-engagement versus control-ambition day. The strongest new paper is a Nature Communications study using individualized transcranial ultrasound stimulation to hit the human globus pallidus internus and read out local field potentials through implanted deep brain stimulation leads. That is rare direct evidence of deep-target engagement from a nominally noninvasive modality. The strongest clinical context paper remains the randomized PTSD trial using individualized functional MRI guidance for transcranial magnetic stimulation, because it continues to set a better-than-usual bar for circuit-based psychiatric targeting. On the computational and network side, I scouted broadly, but most of the newest titles were still stronger as framing material than as preserve-worthy notes.
digests.overview:
The most relevant new paper today is Individualized non-invasive deep brain stimulation of the basal ganglia using transcranial ultrasound stimulation. The useful part is not the phrase non-invasive DBS, which is marketing-dangerous on its face. The useful part is narrower and better: the authors used subject-specific acoustic simulations, targeted the globus pallidus internus in patients who already had implanted DBS systems, and then recorded local field potentials from that deep target while delivering ultrasound. Theta-burst ultrasound increased theta power during stimulation, ten-hertz ultrasound increased beta power, and some effects lasted up to forty minutes. In healthy participants, globus pallidus internus stimulation also worsened stop-signal performance while pulvinar stimulation did not, which at least argues for some target specificity. This does not prove ultrasound is ready to replace implanted DBS. It does show direct human deep-target engagement with physiological and behavioral consequences, which is a materially stronger claim than most ultrasound neuromodulation papers can support.

The second paper worth attention is Personalized fMRI-Guided TMS Targeting the Threat Neurocircuitry in PTSD: A Randomized Clinical Trial. It is not new to the repo anymore, but it remains one of the better recent examples of a psychiatric neuromodulation study trying to make target logic, mechanistic endpoint, and later symptom outcome live in the same trial. Active stimulation reduced right amygdala threat reactivity relative to sham, while delayed symptom outcomes favored active treatment. Skin conductance did not move, and the immediate symptom separation was not clean, so this is not a triumphal precision-psychiatry story. But it is still a more serious targeting paper than most.

The third item is Multimodal branched transport infers anatomically aligned brain reaction maps. This is adjacent inspiration rather than a preserve-worthy note. The idea is to infer routed propagation architectures from multimodal data instead of assuming a fixed network and only optimizing transition cost. That is conceptually aligned with intervention logic, because routing matters for where stimulation effects spread. But at abstract level this still looks more like a mathematical framing paper than a demonstrated neuroscience tool. Interesting, yes. Ready to preserve as a practical note, not yet.

A fourth title that surfaced repeatedly was Counterfactual Analysis of Brain Network Dynamics. I am explicitly not preserving it today. The framing sounds appealing, but at accessible depth it still reads like intervention language wrapped around a Hodge-theoretic decomposition without enough empirical burden-bearing. That may mature into a useful citation later, but today it looks more like theory packaging than something that changes how we would build or evaluate a neuromodulation system.
digests.takeaway: The useful lesson today is that direct target engagement matters more than grand control vocabulary. The ultrasound globus-pallidus paper is worth keeping because it actually measures a deep target while perturbing it and shows some behavioral specificity. The PTSD TMS paper remains useful because it ties target choice to a symptom-relevant circuit instead of generic scalp heuristics. By contrast, several fresh computational-network titles sounded intervention-relevant but still carried more mathematical ambition than empirical burden. So today’s honest pattern is simple: preserve the paper that proves it touched something real, keep the serious circuit-targeting clinical trial as context, and do not let elegant theory language crowd out stronger mechanistic evidence.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-02
digests.theme: Today is a targeting-and-dynamics day. The strongest clinical paper is a randomized PTSD trial using individualized functional MRI guidance to pick a transcranial magnetic stimulation target connected to the right amygdala. The strongest computational paper is JEDI: Jointly Embedded Inference of Neural Dynamics, not because it is immediately intervention-ready, but because it tries to infer shared and condition-specific dynamical structure across tasks instead of fitting one recurrent network per silo. The strongest network-level translational paper remains the pediatric vagus nerve stimulation study on intrinsic network resilience and interictal perturbation, but that note already existed in the repo, so it functions here as confirmation rather than as a new preserve-worthy addition.
digests.overview:
The most relevant new paper today is Personalized fMRI-Guided TMS Targeting the Threat Neurocircuitry in PTSD: A Randomized Clinical Trial. The useful part is not the phrase personalized. The useful part is that the personalization logic is actually tied to a circuit hypothesis: find the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex site with the strongest functional connection to the right amygdala, then test whether low-frequency stimulation changes amygdala threat reactivity and symptoms. The result is not clean triumph. The mechanistic endpoint moved, the immediate autonomic endpoint did not, and the clearest symptom separation appears at follow-up rather than right after treatment. But this is still a better-formulated targeting paper than most psychiatric TMS work.

The second new paper worth preserving is Jointly Embedded Inference of Neural Dynamics. It is adjacent rather than clinical, but it matters because it attacks a real bottleneck in mechanistic modeling: most data-constrained recurrent models are trained condition by condition, which makes cross-task comparison awkward and generalization weak. JEDI proposes a hierarchical embedding over recurrent weights so that condition-specific dynamics live in a shared space. If that framework holds up beyond the abstract, it could be useful for state-transition framing, subject-condition comparison, and eventually for control-oriented modeling.

The third paper worth calling out is Time-Varying Directed Interactions in Functional Brain Networks: Modeling and Validation. This is more methods than intervention, but it is a respectable methods paper because it tries to estimate time-varying directed interactions rather than recycling sliding-window correlation. The multimodal validation, task sensitivity, and clinical application to post-concussion vestibular dysfunction make it more credible than a purely synthetic benchmark paper. Still, it is a directed-connectivity method paper, not a direct neuromodulation result, so it belongs in the useful-but-adjacent bucket.

A fourth paper remains important context rather than a new note: Association of Brain Network Perturbations With Response to Vagus Nerve Stimulation in Children With Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy. It already has a note in the repo, but it still deserves mention because it reinforces the same theme as the PTSD paper and JEDI paper: treatment heterogeneity and intervention logic become more legible when you model networks as dynamic and perturbable rather than as static correlation maps.
digests.takeaway: The useful papers today all refuse static thinking. The PTSD trial treats TMS targeting as a circuit-selection problem tied to amygdala reactivity. JEDI treats neural dynamics as something that should be modeled jointly across tasks and contexts rather than separately memorized. The directed-connectivity paper treats brain networks as time-varying and directional rather than as undirected similarity blobs. Even the already-preserved pediatric VNS paper fits the same pattern: response depends on network resilience to perturbation, not just on baseline labels. So the broader lesson is simple. Better neuromodulation work is moving toward explicit state, circuit, and perturbation logic. The field is still far from clean control theory in humans, but at least the better papers are asking questions in that direction.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-04-01
digests.theme: Today is a model-versus-evidence day. The strongest conceptual paper is a generative virtual-brain preprint for predicting Parkinson's neuromodulation response from resting-state functional MRI, because it at least tries to connect individualized network models to counterfactual treatment estimation instead of throwing another opaque classifier at a tiny cohort. The most practically grounded translational paper is a Parkinson's decoding study that compares noninvasive electroencephalography and invasive electrocorticography for motor-state decoding under deep brain stimulation on and off conditions. The most clinically provocative paper is a long-term post-traumatic stress disorder deep brain stimulation follow-up, but it is only four patients, so the signal is interesting and the overclaim is not.
digests.overview:
The most relevant paper today is Predicting Neuromodulation Outcome for Parkinson's Disease with Generative Virtual Brain Model. If the abstract survives fuller scrutiny, it is one of the cleaner recent attempts to use individualized network modeling for treatment selection rather than mere post hoc biomarker reporting. The attractive part is not the phrase foundation model. The attractive part is the counterfactual logic: pretrain a large generative model of resting-state brain dynamics, adapt it to each patient, then estimate how far stimulation moves that patient toward a healthier state and whether that movement predicts outcome. That is at least the right shape of question.

The second paper worth keeping is Invasive and Non-Invasive Neural Decoding of Motor Performance in Parkinson's Disease for Personalized Deep Brain Stimulation. It is smaller and less glamorous, but it is more honest than many adaptive deep brain stimulation papers because it shows what can and cannot be decoded in a mixed invasive and noninvasive setup, and it explicitly ties the decoding story to behavior under stimulation rather than treating biomarkers as detached trophies.

The third paper is Long-term outcome of subgenual cingulum and uncinate fasciculus deep brain stimulation for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder. This is clinically intriguing because durable improvement in severe post-traumatic stress disorder would matter a lot, and the tract-level target choice is at least mechanistically legible. But the cohort is four patients. So this is a keep-for-context paper, not a settle-the-field paper.
digests.takeaway: The useful papers today share one virtue: they make the intervention logic more explicit. The virtual-brain paper says treatment response should be predicted by how stimulation moves an individualized network model, not just by static biomarkers. The Parkinson's decoding paper says adaptive control needs behavior-linked, patient-specific signals measured under real stimulation conditions, not generic frequency-band mythology. The post-traumatic stress disorder deep brain stimulation follow-up says tract-aware psychiatric targeting may be worth continuing, but it still lives in feasibility-land. So today is less about triumphant evidence than about better-formulated control and targeting questions.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-31
digests.theme: Today is a targeting-logic versus evidence-depth day. The strongest clinical paper is a randomized head-to-head transcranial magnetic stimulation trial in major depression showing that two connectome-derived targets can differentially shift anxiety versus depressive symptom burden. The strongest network paper is a pediatric vagus nerve stimulation study arguing that baseline anterior network integrity and resilience to interictal perturbation help explain who responds. The strongest computational paper is a control-theory preprint that finally tries to put rigorous passivity analysis under seizure suppression rather than merely simulating another closed-loop heuristic. Together they point at the same practical lesson: personalized neuromodulation gets more credible when targetable circuits, state perturbations, and controller assumptions are made explicit rather than hidden inside syndrome labels.
digests.overview:
The most decision-relevant paper today is Circuit-targeted modulation of anxiety symptoms in individuals with major depression: A randomized head-to-head TMS trial because it prospectively tests a symptom-specific connectomic targeting claim instead of selling it retrospectively. The result is useful but not magical: both targets improved depression similarly, while the dorsomedial anxiosomatic target improved anxiety more strongly. That is a real step toward symptom-selective intervention logic, though the sample is still small and the trial is not a full personalization study.

The most mechanistically useful paper is Association of Brain Network Perturbations With Response to Vagus Nerve Stimulation in Children With Drug-Resistant Focal Epilepsy. It does not give a deployable predictor yet, but it is better than generic biomarker fishing because it links response to both baseline alpha-band network organization and post-IED microstate resilience. That makes the heterogeneity story more circuit-legible.

The most conceptually useful paper is Passivity-Based Control of Electrographic Seizures in a Neural Mass Model of Epilepsy. It is still model-land rather than clinic-land, but it does something rare and valuable: it asks whether seizure dynamics in a standard neural mass model are even compatible with a passivity-based feedback design, and what sensor and output redesign choices are mathematically required if they are not.
digests.takeaway: The best work today is trying to earn the word precision by specifying what varies across patients and what exactly a controller or target is supposed to do. The TMS trial suggests symptom-specific circuit targeting may have prospective value, but only modestly and in a small sample. The VNS network paper makes response heterogeneity more intelligible by tying it to anterior network organization and perturbation resilience rather than demographics or seizure topography. The control-theory paper is further from practice, yet useful because it tightens the formal language around seizure suppression. So the field looks strongest when it replaces broad syndromic neuromodulation claims with explicit circuit, perturbation, and control assumptions.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-30
digests.theme: Today is a control-logic versus clinical-proof day. The strongest clinical hit is a randomized phase 3 anterior thalamic deep brain stimulation trial in drug-resistant epilepsy after vagus nerve stimulation failure, but it lands in the awkward zone between clinically meaningful effect sizes and statistically non-superior between-group proof. The strongest computational hit is an arXiv paper arguing that brain stimulation should be framed as stochastic trajectory tracking rather than one-shot state steering. The most useful mechanistic support paper is a beta-oscillation and repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation study showing that timing relative to beta phase matters more than generic stimulation delivery. Together they sharpen the same point: neuromodulation gets more legible when the control objective is explicit, but most of the field still validates the objective weakly.
digests.overview:
The most decision-relevant paper today is Deep brain stimulation of the thalamus for intractable epilepsy (FRANCE study): A randomized clinical trial because it is an actual phase 3 comparison in a hard population that had already failed vagus nerve stimulation. It is clinically important, but it does not cleanly prove superiority over best medical treatment; the between-group p-value misses conventional significance despite a numerically better seizure reduction and responder rate.

The most conceptually useful paper is A new perspective on brain stimulation interventions: Optimal stochastic tracking control of brain network dynamics. It is not treatment evidence, but it is one of the cleaner recent arguments that intervention goals should be framed as synchronizing unhealthy dynamics toward healthy dynamics, not merely forcing one state vector to another at a single time point.

The best mechanistic adjunct is Characterising motor and cognitive contributions of cortical beta oscillations and their modulation with rTMS. It is a healthy-participant study, so no one should over-translate it, but it gives a more explicit account of what beta-frequency stimulation may be doing: lowering a movement-initiation threshold, with stronger effects when timed to the beta down state.
digests.takeaway: The clean lesson today is that better control language is arriving faster than better proof. The epilepsy trial gives real translational signal, but not definitive superiority. The stochastic tracking paper gives a more realistic computational objective for intervention, but remains far from deployable clinical control. The beta-frequency rTMS paper clarifies one plausible mechanism knob, yet only in healthy volunteers. So the field is getting better at saying what it wants stimulation to do over time, but it still too rarely closes the loop from control objective to target engagement to robust patient benefit.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-29
digests.theme: Today is a programming-and-deployment logic day. The best hits are not grand theory papers; they are papers that make neuromodulation decisions more explicit: a multicenter sham-controlled portable HD-tACS trial in depression, a connectome-guided DBS programming paper for Parkinsonian gait dysfunction, and a mechanistic-but-still-clinical Parkinson’s DBS asymmetry paper showing target-dependent rebalancing effects. The useful pattern is that symptom- or state-specific control logic is getting sharper, while a lot of the field still remains thin on prospective validation.
digests.overview: The most decision-relevant paper today is A multicenter randomized clinical trial of portable transcranial alternating current stimulation for major depressive disorder because it is a real sham-controlled multicenter trial rather than the usual tiny stimulation teaser. Pallidal and subthalamic stimulations modulate inter-hemispheric interaction and asymmetry in Parkinson's disease is worth keeping as adjacent mechanistic support: it links target choice to baseline asymmetry direction and to changes in inter-hemispheric coupling, though it is more explanation than actionable control. digests.takeaway: The honest picture today is that neuromodulation gets more useful when the control problem is stated clearly. The portable HD-tACS depression trial matters because it finally tests a scalable noninvasive protocol in a real randomized multicenter design. The connectome-guided gait DBS paper matters because it acknowledges that one symptom may need a different programming objective than another. The Parkinson’s asymmetry paper is a smaller but still useful sign that target effects are not just about mean motor improvement; they can reshape lateralization and network coupling in baseline-dependent ways. The broader lesson is good: explicit optimization and symptom-specific logic are improving faster than our prospective validation standards.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-26
digests.theme: The useful neuromodulation papers today are less about raw efficacy and more about whether the intervention logic is legible. The strongest work either (a) ties outcome prediction to an actually recorded circuit signal, (b) makes targeting variability explicit instead of pretending scalp heuristics are precise, or (c) shows a manipulable mechanism at the cell/circuit level. The tFUS rat paper is adjacent rather than translational, but it is one of the cleaner recent mechanism papers because it links parameter regime to bidirectional circuit effects and identifies a specific cell-type contribution. A depression “common therapeutic network” paper is worth noting mainly as framing/citation material; it is ambitious and interesting, but much of the causal language outruns what secondary network mapping can really support.
digests.takeaway: The real pattern today is that the better papers are forcing neuromodulation to become more explicit about control variables. The BNST-DBS study says: here is the signal, here is how it predicts outcome, here is how it moves with stimulation. The TMS modeling paper says: here is why your supposed target is not reliably the same target across people. The tFUS paper says: here are the parameter regimes and neuronal populations behind opposite effects. That is the right direction. By contrast, the common-network depression paper is interesting synthesis but still too inferential to carry much mechanistic weight on its own.

digests.title: Neuro Daily — 2026-03-25
digests.theme: Personalized neuromodulation is slowly becoming more real: invasive mapping and adaptive control papers are starting to specify where, when, and why to stimulate instead of just reporting another average effect size. The good work is still narrow and early. The weak work still loves grandiose claims.
digests.overview: Today’s strongest hit is an OCD paper because it actually links target selection, symptom-linked physiology, and downstream circuit engagement in the same patient. The Parkinson adaptive DBS trial matters because it moves aDBS from short in-clinic demos toward longer at-home use, though the endpoint framing is softer than one would like. The closed-loop tACS-fMRI paper is an interesting noninvasive proof of concept, but the sample is tiny and the behavioral gain is modest. A computational paper on DSR+MPC is worth preserving as adjacent inspiration, not as evidence for deployable intervention design.
digests.takeaway: The useful pattern across today’s papers is that the serious work is converging on a simple requirement: if you claim precision neuromodulation, you should be able to specify a target, a state signal, and evidence that stimulation changes that signal in the predicted direction. The OCD mapping paper does this best, albeit in one patient. The Parkinson aDBS trial shows that chronic sensing-driven stimulation is operationally viable at scale, but the control logic is still relatively simple and the endpoint framing is not pristine. The tACS-fMRI study is a real proof of concept for individualized noninvasive optimization, though still far from a durable translational result. The DSR+MPC paper is most useful as a hypothesis engine for which states or regions may be controllable, not as evidence that we can already steer psychiatric state spaces cleanly.

notes.title: Deep brain stimulation reduces subthalamic nucleus pathological dynamics and rescues gait deficits associated with dopamine loss
notes.whySelected: It is a mechanistically useful DBS paper because it ties therapeutic benefit to changes in pathological beta-rhythmic spiking and network synchrony rather than to generic stimulation effects.
notes.verdictText: This is worth preserving because it treats Parkinsonian gait rescue as a circuit-dynamics problem, not as a black-box clinical output. The paper is preclinical and obviously cannot answer the full human therapy question, but it does the right mechanistic thing: simultaneous multi-neuron recording in subthalamic nucleus during locomotion, with intermittent DBS in healthy and dopamine-depleted mice. The main limitation is transfer. Mouse gait and intermittent experimental DBS are not the same thing as chronic human therapy.
notes.overview: The authors record multi-neuron activity from the subthalamic nucleus in healthy and dopamine-depleted mice during voluntary locomotion and ask how dopamine loss changes movement encoding and how deep brain stimulation alters those pathological dynamics. According to the abstract, dopamine depletion worsens gait, exaggerates population-level movement encoding, increases movement-related spiking, and elevates beta-rhythmic firing at rest. Intermittent DBS suppresses firing in both healthy and dopamine-depleted animals, but in the dopamine-depleted state it also selectively reduces beta-rhythmic spiking, desynchronizes the subthalamic network, and rescues gait deficits. The useful point is that DBS benefit is linked to reduction of pathological dynamics, not just to indiscriminate activation or inhibition.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is exactly the sort of paper that makes DBS mechanism less mystical. The intervention is not just “stimulate here and the animal moves better.” The intervention appears to reduce a specific pathological dynamical regime, which is a much better design language.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a strong mechanistic DBS reference. It is preclinical, but it does real explanatory work and supports a cleaner pathological-dynamics account of therapeutic stimulation.

notes.title: A walk-sum framework of frequency-dependent brain communication architecture
notes.whySelected: It is one of the cleaner recent attempts to derive frequency-specific large-scale brain communication structure analytically from connectome topology instead of layering on under-identified dynamical decoration.
notes.verdictText: This is the strongest paper of the day because it offers real mechanism at the level of communication architecture, not just another descriptive band-power story. The central claim is ambitious but disciplined: a topology-derived resolvent already predicts the spatial organization of frequency-dependent communication channels, and the authors then test that claim across large MEG datasets plus intracranial EEG. The main risk is overconfidence in analytical elegance; the real question is how much this framework survives alternative preprocessing, parcellation, and dynamical assumptions.
notes.overview: The paper asks why particular frequency bands preferentially express particular large-scale communication patterns in the brain. Rather than beginning with a richly parameterized neural-mass model, the authors derive a frequency-dependent transfer function from the walk-sum algebra of the structural connectome and argue that its spatial structure follows directly from graph topology. According to the abstract, the bare resolvent with zero free parameters predicts a parcellation-invariant crossover near 12.6 hertz and matches eigenmode structure with very high correlation, while a lightly parameterized dressed resolvent improves prediction further. These predictions are then checked against source-reconstructed MEG from 912 people across three datasets and intracranial EEG from 90 epilepsy patients, with additional perturbational relevance coming from propofol and schizophrenia examples. If the claims hold, the paper matters because it turns frequency-specific communication from descriptive phenomenology into something closer to a constrained graph-theoretic object.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it offers a cleaner foundation for frequency-aware intervention logic. If different bands preferentially recruit different graph channels for principled topological reasons, then frequency selection should be treated as part of targeting rather than as an afterthought.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a core network-computational reference. Even if some quantitative claims soften under full-text inspection, the paper is doing real conceptual work and could improve how future stimulation and observation problems are framed.

notes.title: A functional MRI and magnetoencephalography study of the cognitive modulatory effect of transcranial direct current stimulation in early Alzheimer's disease
notes.whySelected: It is a decent human multimodal follow-up paper because it tries to relate left DLPFC tDCS in early Alzheimer's disease to specific resting-state, task-fMRI, and MEG changes instead of reporting cognition alone.
notes.verdictText: This is worth keeping, but not overrating. The multimodal imaging package is genuinely more informative than a bare behavioral tDCS study, and the posterior-cingulate plus entorhinal findings are at least mechanistically suggestive. But the intervention logic remains soft because the accessible evidence is pre-post and the abstract does not make a strong sham-controlled causal design visible.
notes.overview: The paper studies forty patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild Alzheimer's disease and examines brain functional changes accompanying anodal transcranial direct current stimulation over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Using resting-state fMRI, task-based fMRI during episodic memory operations, and resting MEG, the authors report reduced left middle frontal connectivity with precuneus and posterior cingulate after stimulation, increased posterior cingulate and right middle frontal activation during memory tasks, reduced right occipital gamma power, and increased theta-phase to gamma-amplitude coupling in the left entorhinal cortex. The multimodal pattern suggests that prefrontal stimulation may alter memory-relevant large-scale and mesial temporal dynamics, but the paper is better read as accompaniment evidence than as decisive proof of therapeutic efficacy.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a useful reminder that even middling human stimulation papers become more valuable when they expose network and oscillatory accompaniments. The paper is not decisive, but it is better than pure score-chasing.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a secondary human reference. Useful for multimodal framing, but not strong enough to anchor a precision-stimulation argument on its own.

notes.title: Structural and Functional Connectivity Predict the Effects of Direct Brain Stimulation on Memory
notes.whySelected: It makes a clean argument that adaptive timing only helps when the stimulated site is structurally embedded in the right memory network.
notes.verdictText: This is a preserve note because it adds a missing piece to closed-loop stimulation logic. The field often frames timing and targeting as separate design questions, but this paper says they interact: classifier-triggered stimulation can work on average, yet benefit depends strongly on the structural network context of the stimulated site. The main caution is that the connectivity analysis is normative rather than patient-specific, so the precision story is still only half-finished.
notes.overview: The authors analyze intracranial stimulation data from adults with medically refractory epilepsy performing a verbal delayed free-recall task. Across sixty-one sessions, they compare closed-loop stimulation delivered during classifier-detected poor encoding states with random stimulation and then ask whether variability in memory benefit can be explained by the network embedding of the stimulated left temporal cortex sites. Normative diffusion tractography and functional connectivity maps suggest that sites with stronger structural coupling to a distributed fronto-temporo-parietal verbal-encoding network produce larger memory gains, while functional connectivity shows weaker and less robust regional associations. The useful contribution is not a generic connectomics layer pasted onto stimulation data. It is the claim that adaptive timing is necessary but insufficient unless the stimulation target is also structurally positioned inside the computation one wants to rescue.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it sharpens a general design rule for closed-loop neuromodulation: good triggers do not rescue a bad target. If the stimulated node is not embedded in the relevant network scaffold, adaptivity alone will not buy much.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as highly relevant. This is a strong intervention-logic paper because it makes targeting and timing answer to the same mechanistic frame.

notes.title: Low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound amygdala neuromodulation: a double-blind sham-controlled target engagement study and unblinded single-arm clinical trial
notes.whySelected: It is one of the rare noninvasive psychiatry papers that pairs patient-level deep-target engagement with a repeated-treatment protocol instead of jumping straight from feasibility to hype.
notes.verdictText: This is not a clean efficacy trial, because the treatment phase is open-label and therefore fragile to expectancy and nonspecific improvement. But it still deserves a preserve note because the paper does the two things the field usually separates: it first shows target engagement at the amygdala under sham control, then runs a short repeated-treatment study in a relevant patient group. For direct noninvasive subcortical neuromodulation in psychiatry, that is a meaningful step forward.
notes.overview: The study targets the left amygdala with MRI-guided low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound in people with mood, anxiety, and trauma-related disorders. In the first phase, the authors use a double-blind within-subject sham-controlled tFUS during fMRI design to ask whether active sonication changes amygdala and broader circuit responses acutely. In the second phase, the patient cohort receives fifteen sessions of repetitive tFUS over three weeks in an unblinded single-arm treatment protocol to assess safety, feasibility, symptom change, and pre-post change in amygdala reactivity to emotional faces. Active versus sham ultrasound reduced left-amygdala BOLD signal and produced patient-related hippocampal and insular differences; the repeated-treatment phase was reportedly well tolerated and associated with symptom improvement and reduced amygdala activation to emotional stimuli. The real value is not that efficacy is settled. It is that the paper treats deep-target engagement as part of the therapeutic claim instead of an optional decoration.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is exactly the kind of paper that can sharpen standards for deep noninvasive psychiatry. It says the right thing implicitly: if you want to claim subcortical therapeutic modulation, you should show subcortical engagement and then test whether repeated dosing is even plausible.
notes.finalDecision: Strong keep. This is one of the more credible recent translational papers for direct noninvasive subcortical neuromodulation in psychiatry, even though the therapeutic efficacy claim remains preliminary.

notes.title: Beyond where: When and how brain stimulation drives state transitions
notes.whySelected: It asks a much better targeting question than usual by treating stimulation response as a property of subject-specific dynamics rather than static anatomy alone.
notes.verdictText: This is a strong keep for framing and mechanism, even though it is still a modeling paper rather than an intervention validation paper. The central move is good: the best target for changing brain state may not be the anatomically obvious region, but the node sitting in the right dynamical regime at the right frequency and state. The weakness is the usual one for this literature: elegant whole-brain modeling can outrun empirical identifiability if validation is thin.
notes.overview: The paper uses subject-specific whole-brain Hopf models fitted to MEG data across five canonical frequency bands to study why some regions respond more strongly to stimulation and which nodes are best for driving transitions between brain states. Rather than assuming that an auditory task transition should be driven from auditory cortex or that a target can be chosen from anatomical labels alone, the authors test whether responsiveness depends on system dynamics. Their reported answer is yes: regions with smaller oscillation radius and greater temporal variability respond more strongly, and the determinants of responsiveness differ by state and frequency band, with slower frequencies more phase-driven and faster frequencies more dependent on network synchrony. The main value is that it re-centers neuromodulation around dynamical controllability rather than cartographic folklore.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it offers a cleaner conceptual frame for precision neuromodulation. Instead of asking only which named region is relevant, it asks which node is controllable in the current dynamical landscape. That is much closer to an actual intervention theory.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as highly relevant. Even if some modeling details soften under full inspection, the paper improves the control logic of how stimulation targets should be conceptualized.

notes.title: White matter pathways mediating dorsolateral prefrontal TMS therapy for depression
notes.whySelected: It tries to replace depression-TMS targeting folklore with an explicit structural communication-path account linking dorsolateral prefrontal stimulation sites to subgenual cingulate through multi-step routes.
notes.verdictText: This is a compact but important paper because it pushes TMS targeting away from one-number resting-connectivity rhetoric and toward a mechanistic pathway story. The accessible text is too thin to treat the method as fully validated, but the core framing is strong: route geometry through the connectome may matter more than sloganized anti-subgenual correlation. That is exactly the sort of shift the field needs.
notes.overview: The authors use connectome modeling to infer putative polysynaptic cortical and subcortical pathways linking dorsolateral prefrontal cortex TMS sites to the subgenual cingulate cortex through intermediate regions. Their headline claim is that route length along these proposed pathways explains antidepressant response in two independent patient cohorts and also explains the clinical efficacy of functional-MRI-guided TMS targeting. The useful read is not that structural-pathway modeling now solves precision TMS. The useful read is that stimulation efficacy may depend on how well the chosen cortical site can communicate with deeper depression-relevant circuitry through anatomically plausible routes. That makes the paper a meaningful mechanistic upgrade over simple site-to-sgACC connectivity heuristics.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it sharpens intervention logic. If depression TMS efficacy depends on traversable communication routes rather than just on static connectivity slogans, that changes how we should think about targeting, mechanistic baselines, and what counts as a serious personalization claim.
notes.finalDecision: Preserve. Even from abstract-level inspection, this looks like a meaningful framing upgrade for depression TMS targeting, though it still needs harder comparison against simpler baselines and more direct validation of the proposed propagation story.

notes.title: Low-intensity focused ultrasound to human amygdala reveals a causal role in ambiguous emotion processing and alters local and network activity
notes.whySelected: It provides rare human evidence that low-intensity focused ultrasound can causally perturb a deep affective target and produce convergent behavioral, connectivity, and spectroscopy changes.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the cleanest recent human focused-ultrasound papers because it does more than report a behavioral blip after sonication. It couples target engagement to resting-state connectivity and metabolite evidence, uses both sham and control-target conditions, and asks a psychologically legible question about emotional ambiguity. It is still a healthy-volunteer mechanistic study, not a psychiatric treatment paper, but the causal-perturbation value is high.
notes.overview: The authors used offline low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound stimulation to modulate the bilateral basolateral amygdala in healthy volunteers, with separate mid-insula and sham sessions as controls. After stimulation, participants completed an emotional-learning task and underwent seven-tesla resting-state imaging plus spectroscopy-style target-engagement assessment. Basolateral-amygdala stimulation reduced the target’s resting-state connectivity fingerprint, lowered its excitation-inhibition balance, increased approach toward neutral emotionally ambiguous faces in a stimulation-volume-dependent manner, and slowed responses to neutral and happy faces. The real value is not simply that ultrasound reached a deep structure. It is that the paper triangulates target engagement and behavior tightly enough to make a credible causal claim about amygdala involvement in ambiguity resolution.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is the kind of deep noninvasive perturbation paper that actually earns mechanistic attention. It provides a concrete example of how to join target engagement, behavior, and circuit interpretation rather than hand-waving about ultrasound’s future.
notes.finalDecision: Strong keep. This is a must-read mechanistic paper for focused ultrasound and affective-circuit perturbation, even though it is still an early-stage human experimental study rather than translational proof.

notes.title: A deep representation learning model to predict response to vagus nerve stimulation
notes.whySelected: It starts from the failure of presurgical clinical predictors and then uses routine structural MRI plus deep representation learning to produce a more biologically anchored VNS response model.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the better recent predictive-neuromodulation papers because it does not pretend standard clinical variables already solve the problem. The model performance is not miraculous, but an AUC around 0.73 on routine presurgical T1 MRI is meaningful in a domain where baseline clinical prediction is near useless. The main caution is the usual one: biologically flavored interpretability is not the same thing as causal mechanism.
notes.overview: The paper introduces VQ-VNS, a deep representation learning model that predicts pediatric vagus nerve stimulation response from preoperative T1-weighted MRI. The setup is notable for its honesty about the baseline. In the largest reported pediatric VNS cohort, presurgical clinical variables produced almost no predictive signal. The authors then pretrain on thousands of structural MRIs to learn compact anatomical representations and use those representations to predict later response, reporting an AUC of 0.73 in an imaging cohort of 263 patients. Their interpretation layer localizes predictive signal to serotonin-rich regions and links nonresponse to broader network disruption. The right read is not that the paper has solved VNS selection, but that it shows routine anatomy may contain response-relevant structure that easy clinical covariates fail to capture.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a serious attempt to connect routine anatomy, predictive modeling, and intervention selection. It treats heterogeneity as something to model from real brain structure rather than something to hand-wave after surgery.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. This is a strong preserve note for VNS response modeling: not clinically definitive, but much better than decorative predictor work because it uses practical input data, a serious negative baseline, and some biologically interpretable structure.

notes.title: Predictive value of subgenual cingulate normative connectivity to TMS treatment site for antidepressant response in routine clinical practice: a prospective, multisite cohort study
notes.whySelected: It is a valuable real-world pressure test of the anti-subgenual TMS targeting heuristic and finds that normative connectivity alone explains little in a heterogeneous clinic sample.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the more useful recent depression-TMS papers precisely because the main result is mostly negative. In a prospective multisite routine-practice cohort, normative connectivity from the delivered left-DLPFC TMS site to subgenual cingulate did not meaningfully predict symptom improvement on its own. That does not invalidate network targeting, but it does weaken the habit of talking as if anti-subgenual targeting is already a robust standalone personalization rule.
notes.overview: The paper asks whether one of the best-known precision-TMS ideas actually survives contact with routine clinical heterogeneity. Sixty-six patients with major depressive disorder received three to eight weeks of standard-care left-DLPFC repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation, with actual stimulation sites recorded on multiple days using MRI neuronavigation. The authors then estimated each site’s functional connectivity to subgenual cingulate using a large normative resting-state dataset from healthy individuals and tested whether that connectivity predicted change in Beck Depression Inventory scores. The main answer is no: the primary association was null, while baseline anxiety and psychiatric comorbidity explained more variance once added in post-hoc models. The paper matters because it separates a plausible targeting story from a clinically reliable one.
notes.whyItMatters: Because cabbageland cares about intervention logic, not target folklore. This paper is useful exactly because it shows that a mechanistically plausible network story can still be too weak or too partial to govern clinical personalization on its own.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. This is not a triumphant precision-targeting paper, and that is exactly why it is valuable.

notes.title: Controlling the human connectome with spatially diffuse input signals
notes.whySelected: It upgrades network control theory in a way that better matches real neuromodulation by modeling spatially spread inputs instead of perfectly local node-wise stimulation.
notes.verdictText: This is a strong computational-network paper because it improves the control model at exactly the place where many neurostimulation interpretations become unrealistic. Instead of assuming each input acts on a single isolated node, the paper lets control inputs spread spatially with distance decay, which better reflects cortical continuity and the blur of actual stimulation technologies. The result is not a therapy recipe, but it is a useful upgrade for any intervention logic built on brain-state control arguments.
notes.overview: The paper addresses a mismatch between standard network control theory and real brain stimulation. Classic optimal-control formulations often assume that one can inject control independently into single network nodes, but real cortex is spatially continuous and most stimulation methods spread beyond a point target. The authors therefore adapt control models so an input centered on one region also influences nearby regions with an exponentially decaying spatial profile. Across empirically derived brain states, this more realistic spatial-input model lowers the energy required for transitions, often allows the same control effect to be approximated with far fewer input signals, and yields input-density maps that correspond to independent functional, metabolic, genetic, and neurochemical annotations. The useful contribution is not clinical proof. It is a more plausible control formalism for thinking about how whole-brain state transitions might actually be driven.
notes.whyItMatters: Because cabbageland cares about intervention logic that survives contact with physics. This paper is useful as a conceptual upgrade: if the control model assumes a point actuator that no real device has, downstream targeting claims may already be off by construction.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. This is not a therapy paper, but it is exactly the sort of modeling note that can sharpen future stimulation framing, targeting logic, and mechanistic critique.

notes.title: Causal connectivity maps derived from single-pulse interleaved TMS/fMRI
notes.whySelected: It is a useful methods paper because it tries to turn image-guided TMS from resting-connectivity inference into stimulation-evoked causal circuit mapping.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the better recent targeting-method papers because it makes a more causal move than the usual correlational network-mapping workflow. The useful claim is not that it finds a clinically validated psychiatric target. The useful claim is that personalized TMS plus interleaved fMRI can generate reproducible downstream circuit maps after controlling for pain, motion, and somatosensory confounds.
notes.overview: The paper aims to map causal downstream responses to personalized cortical stimulation sites rather than relying only on resting-state functional connectivity. In more than eighty participants, the authors selected left-hemisphere targets intended to engage either subgenual anterior cingulate cortex or basolateral amygdala and then delivered single-pulse TMS during fMRI. They quantified voxelwise TMS-evoked BOLD responses and residualized major nuisance factors such as head motion, pain, and somatosensory effects. The main result is that frontal targets aimed at subgenual circuits elicited subgenual and distributed downstream responses, while ventrolateral targets aimed at amygdala circuits elicited negative BOLD responses in the amygdala and broad downstream engagement. The most useful output is the public causal-connectivity map resource, not a claim that the psychiatric targeting problem is solved.
notes.whyItMatters: Because cabbageland is interested in interventions that can be justified mechanistically rather than by decorative network rhetoric. This paper is useful as an infrastructure step toward more causal targeting logic.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. Strong methods value, good causal-targeting infrastructure value, and worth citing whenever resting-connectivity targeting is being treated as if it were enough.

notes.title: cuBNM: GPU-Accelerated Brain Network Modeling
notes.whySelected: It is worth keeping because individualized whole-brain modeling only starts to matter for targeting and mechanism once fitting stops being so computationally expensive that almost nobody can use it seriously.
notes.verdictText: This is infrastructure, not intervention evidence, so it should not be romanticized. But it addresses a real bottleneck in computational neuro: individualized brain-network-model fitting is often too slow to be operationally useful. If the reported speedups hold in ordinary practice, this kind of tooling could make personalized modeling less decorative and more testable.
notes.overview: The paper introduces cuBNM, a GPU-accelerated Python package for simulating and fitting large-scale brain network models. The main claim is straightforward: parallel execution on graphics processors can speed simulations by several hundred times relative to central processors, making both group-level and individualized fitting more tractable for low- and high-dimensional models. The authors illustrate this with optimization workflows, model-fit analyses, and examples using Human Connectome Project data to examine reliability and heritability of simulated and empirical features. The paper matters less because it is fast and more because it makes a class of mechanistic modeling workflows more realistically usable at cohort scale.
notes.whyItMatters: Because personalized neuromodulation logic keeps running into the same wall: subject-specific models are easy to praise and hard to deploy. Work like this matters if it helps move individualized modeling from prestigious side-analysis to something that could actually sit inside a targeting workflow.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as useful infrastructure. It is not evidence that whole-brain models already guide better neuromodulation, but it meaningfully lowers one of the barriers to testing that claim.

notes.title: Frequency-Dependent Whole-Brain Reconfiguration Following Left DLPFC rTMS in Older Adults: A 106-Channel fNIRS Study
notes.whySelected: It is a useful network-level rTMS paper because it measures distributed immediate reconfiguration in older adults and explicitly shows that the standard one-hertz-versus-ten-hertz story is too coarse.
notes.verdictText: This is not a clinical efficacy result and it is not strong enough to settle mechanism. But it is worth keeping because it looks at the right unit of analysis: whole-brain network response rather than target folklore. The paper is especially useful because it reports both the expected broad frequency split and the awkward local exceptions that simpler stimulation narratives usually hide.
notes.overview: The study asks how one-hertz and ten-hertz repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex immediately reshape resting-state whole-brain connectivity in healthy older adults. Thirty participants aged sixty to seventy-five completed both stimulation conditions in a randomized single-blind crossover design, with one-hundred-and-six-channel functional near-infrared spectroscopy before and after each visit. At summary-network level, ten hertz was associated with more positive changes in global topology and spatially distributed connectivity, while one hertz tended in the opposite direction. But the more interesting result is that local exceptions remained, including bilateral primary-motor-cortex effects that ran against the crude frequency rule. The paper therefore helps mainly as a network-reconfiguration caution against binary stimulation slogans.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is exactly the kind of paper that pushes intervention reasoning from recipe language toward network language. It does not solve targeting, but it does help break the lazy habit of acting as though frequency labels are already mechanism.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a useful network-level neuromodulation note. It is not clinically decisive, but it is a good corrective to oversimplified rTMS mechanism talk.

notes.title: mPFC axons drive cognitive control enhancement during striatal stimulation
notes.whySelected: It asks the right mechanistic question for psychiatric stimulation by separating recruited cortical afferents from local striatal neurons instead of treating the target as a magical anatomical blob.
notes.verdictText: This is a preserve note because it makes ventral-striatal-style stimulation more mechanistically legible. The key result is a dissociation: optogenetic stimulation of medial-prefrontal axons in the striatum reproduced the response-time benefit seen with electrical stimulation, while sustained stimulation of local striatal neurons impaired performance. The main caution is that this is still a rodent preprint built around a cognitive proxy task, so it is a mechanism paper, not clinical proof.
notes.overview: The paper studies which neural elements drive the cognitive-control benefits previously associated with ventral internal capsule or ventral striatal stimulation. In a rodent set-shift task, the authors compare high-frequency optogenetic stimulation of medial prefrontal cortex axons terminating in the mid-striatum against stimulation of local mid-striatal neurons. Stimulation of the cortical axons reduced response times and matched the cognitive enhancement previously seen with electrical stimulation, whereas stimulation of local neurons worsened performance when sustained for more than ten minutes. The paper also reports time-dependent decline in the axonal stimulation benefit alongside attenuation of local evoked responses and reduced post-stimulation circuit responsiveness, suggesting that both the useful effect and its decay are circuit-specific rather than generic arousal.
notes.whyItMatters: Because too much psychiatric neuromodulation language still treats the target as if an atlas label explained the mechanism. This paper is useful precisely because it says no: what matters may be the recruited cortical afferents, not the local striatal neurons. That is much closer to an intervention logic that can inform targeting and control.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a highly relevant mechanistic translational note. It does not prove psychiatric efficacy, but it makes the target logic substantially less vague.

notes.title: Treatment of Persisting Symptoms after Concussion with Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation: A Double-Blinded, Randomized, Controlled Trial
notes.whySelected: It is a useful negative clinical trial showing that a plausible high-frequency left-dorsolateral-prefrontal rTMS protocol did not beat sham for persistent post-concussion symptoms.
notes.verdictText: This is worth preserving because clean negative trials are more informative than endless pilot positivity. Ninety-one participants were randomized, the protocol was substantial, and the primary result was still null: active rTMS did not significantly outperform sham on the main post-concussion symptom outcome at post-treatment, one month, or three months. The paper does not kill neuromodulation for concussion, but it does undercut generic DLPFC recipe transfer and should raise the bar for symptom-specific or state-dependent designs.
notes.overview: The trial tests whether twenty sessions of high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex improve persistent symptoms after mild traumatic brain injury better than sham. Adults with symptoms lasting at least three months and up to five years post-injury were randomized one-to-one to active or sham treatment. The primary outcome was change in Rivermead Postconcussion Symptoms Questionnaire score from baseline to post-treatment and then one- and three-month follow-up. Both groups improved over time, but there was no significant between-group difference at any primary endpoint. Secondary measures including depression, anxiety, quality of life, headache, cognition, and post-traumatic stress showed time effects but not group effects.
notes.whyItMatters: Because negative intervention evidence is part of good mechanism. If a plausible protocol fails, that is a clue that the disorder or syndrome is not well matched to the chosen target and timing logic. This paper is a decent antidote to neuromodulation theater.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a useful negative clinical note. The result is not exciting, but it is exactly the kind of evidence that keeps future intervention framing honest.

notes.title: Precision phase targeting of event-related oscillations using real-time closed-loop TMS-EEG
notes.whySelected: It addresses a real closed-loop bottleneck by moving from phase prediction in clean periodic rhythms toward direct online targeting of brief event-related oscillations.
notes.verdictText: This is a preserve note because the engineering problem is real and intervention-relevant. Most phase-locked stimulation stacks work best when the underlying rhythm is stable and periodic; this paper tries to make phase targeting work for transient, task-linked activity instead. The main limitation is that validation here was done on simulated sine waves and human EEG without active TMS delivery, so the difficult artifact-heavy online regime still remains to be earned.
notes.overview: The paper presents a real-time closed-loop TMS-EEG system that directly detects oscillatory phase rather than predicting it from a previously observed rhythm. The authors argue that prediction-based systems depend too heavily on periodic signals and therefore struggle when the target is a brief event-related oscillation. They validate the direct-detection system against a prediction-based baseline using simulated data and human EEG recordings from eighteen participants, including occipital alpha rhythms and event-related theta during spatial navigation tasks. Across these tests, the new system reportedly increases trigger probability and reduces phase-error variability, especially for transient task-related theta. The point is not that the stimulation problem is solved. The point is that the timing layer may be getting good enough to target cognitive events rather than only steady rhythms.
notes.whyItMatters: Because closed-loop neuromodulation rhetoric often sounds sophisticated while the timing stack underneath it is fragile. This paper matters if it helps move stimulation from generic periodic entrainment toward intervention on brief state transitions and task-linked computations.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a highly relevant methods-and-control note. The paper does not yet close the physiological loop, but it improves a real bottleneck in that direction.

notes.title: Brain Functional Connectivity Signatures of Craving Across Substance Use Disorders: A Transdiagnostic Approach
notes.whySelected: It tries to derive a transdiagnostic network biomarker of craving instead of staying trapped in single-substance silos.
notes.verdictText: This is worth keeping because the authors at least attempt the right abstraction level. Instead of building a craving model inside one diagnosis and pretending it generalizes, they use connectome-based predictive modeling across cannabis, opioid, and tobacco use disorders and then test the resulting network in external alcohol and smoking datasets. The main caveat is that this remains resting-state prediction, so it is still much closer to biomarker association than intervention-ready mechanism.
notes.overview: The paper uses resting-state functional MRI to build a distributed predictive network for subjective craving across multiple substance use disorders. In a transdiagnostic training sample of seventy-eight participants with cannabis, opioid, or tobacco use disorder, the authors apply connectome-based predictive modeling to identify a network whose connectivity predicts self-reported craving. Computational lesion analysis suggests important contributions from the right medial orbitofrontal cortex, right dorsal posterior cingulate cortex, and left lateral medial frontal gyrus. The authors then test the network in two external settings: alcohol-dependent patients and smokers. According to the abstract, the network predicts distinct cognitive and motivational craving components in alcohol dependence and also predicts abstinence-related craving and within-person craving change in smokers.
notes.whyItMatters: Because transdiagnostic psychiatry is only useful when it produces better intervention or prediction logic rather than broader vagueness. This paper is not there yet, but it is closer than diagnosis-silo work that rediscovers the same craving story separately for every substance.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a useful adjacent network-psychiatry note. It is stronger than ordinary resting-state biomarker packaging, but it is still several steps away from intervention-ready mechanism.

notes.title: Successful Closed-Loop Neurofeedback Alpha Frequency Modulation Enhances the Temporal Dynamics of Attention
notes.whySelected: It provides relatively clean causal leverage on alpha timing by showing that successful closed-loop neurofeedback can shift individual alpha frequency and alter the temporal deployment of attention.
notes.verdictText: This is a strong healthy-participant oscillation paper rather than a clinical intervention result. It earns a keep because it does more than correlate alpha with attention. It separates learners from non-learners, uses an active placebo control, and ties behavioral change to shorter alpha desynchronization latency. The limitation is that neurofeedback learner effects always invite selection and mechanism questions.
notes.overview: The paper asks whether changing individual alpha frequency through EEG-based closed-loop neurofeedback can causally alter attentional timing. Across five sessions in one hundred eight healthy adults, participants attempted to increase parieto-occipital individual alpha frequency while an active placebo group provided a stronger comparison than usual. Participants who successfully learned to increase alpha frequency showed faster responses, better attentional efficiency, stronger cue-related facilitation, and shorter alpha event-related desynchronization latencies than non-learners and placebo participants. Repeated-measures mediation suggested that neurofeedback-related alpha-frequency increases partly improved response speed through earlier desynchronization timing. The useful read is that alpha frequency looks more like a tunable control parameter for attentional readiness than a passive correlate.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it sharpens the idea that oscillatory parameters can be intervention targets rather than mere biomarkers. That is useful for any project that cares about timing, readiness, and state-dependent control.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. It is not a clinical breakthrough, but it is a good mechanistic oscillation-control paper with more causal bite than most alpha-attention work.

notes.title: Regulation of Autism-Related Self-Injurious Behavior by Electrical Stimulation of Corticostriatal Circuits in Mice and Humans
notes.whySelected: It is one of the cleaner recent attempts to argue that severe self-injurious behavior in autism sits inside a controllable fronto-limbic-striatal circuit rather than being treated as desperate symptom management.
notes.verdictText: This is a serious translational paper because it tries to connect intervention, circuit, and behavior across species. The strongest part is not just that nucleus accumbens stimulation reduced pathology-like behavior in mice and was associated with improvement in children. The strongest part is that the authors try to map a therapeutic locus and broader fronto-limbic-striatal network rather than selling a target by vibe alone. The obvious limit is that the human side is still very small and highly selected.
notes.overview: The paper studies whether electrical stimulation of the nucleus accumbens can regulate severe self-injurious behavior by modulating corticostriatal circuitry. In an autism-relevant BTBR mouse model, chronic bilateral nucleus accumbens stimulation reduced injurious self-grooming, improved grooming-pattern organization, and reduced repetitive marble-burying without obvious effects on general locomotion, anxiety-like behavior, or social-chamber time. In children with profound autism and severe, refractory self-injurious behavior undergoing nucleus-accumbens deep brain stimulation, the authors identify a therapeutic sweet spot within the target, associate better improvement with sensorimotor, limbic, and striatal connectivity, and report longitudinal structural changes in fronto-limbic-striatal regions. The useful read is that the paper makes a circuit argument. The non-useful read would be to pretend it establishes a ready-for-scale clinical therapy.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is one of the more convincing recent examples of neuromodulation trying to earn a mechanistic claim in an extremely hard behavioral domain. It sharpens how to talk about severe-behavior intervention as circuit control rather than target branding.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. This is not enough evidence to declare nucleus-accumbens deep brain stimulation an established therapy for severe self-injurious behavior in autism, but it is enough to preserve as a strong translational circuit paper.

notes.title: Deep Transcranial Ultrasound Stimulation Using Personalized Acoustic Metamaterials Improves Treatment-Resistant Depression in Humans
notes.whySelected: It is one of the more serious recent noninvasive deep-target neuromodulation papers because it treats individualized acoustic correction and tract-level targeting as core problems rather than details to hand-wave away.
notes.verdictText: This is still a tiny open-label pilot, so the clinical efficacy claim should stay on a short leash. But it is worth preserving because it attacks the real bottleneck in deep noninvasive ultrasound neuromodulation: skull distortion and individualized targeting. That makes it more valuable than many ultrasound papers that promise deep precision while being vague about the physical path to it.
notes.overview: The paper presents a portable neuronavigated transcranial ultrasound system that uses patient-specific acoustic metamaterials, or metalenses, to correct skull-induced aberrations and target white-matter tracts of the subcallosal cingulate in treatment-resistant depression. Five participants underwent a dense five-day course of twenty-five five-minute stimulation sessions. The authors report no serious adverse events, an average depression-severity reduction of about sixty-one percent by day five, four of five responders, and two remissions. The useful read is not that ultrasound depression treatment is solved. The useful read is that individualized physical targeting of deep depression circuitry may be becoming plausible enough to test seriously in larger controlled studies.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it raises the standard for noninvasive deep-target claims. It suggests that if ultrasound is going to become a serious psychiatric neuromodulation tool, individualized physical correction and targeting may be essential rather than optional.
notes.finalDecision: Keep. The efficacy signal is far too preliminary to trust at face value, but the targeting and device logic are strong enough to preserve.

notes.title: Channel Capacity for Time-Resolved Effective Connectivity in Functional Neuroimaging
notes.whySelected: It proposes a directed, time-resolved information-transfer metric that is closer to state-transition reasoning than ordinary dynamic functional connectivity.
notes.verdictText: This is a methods paper worth preserving because it attacks a real problem in network neuroscience: dynamic connectivity estimates are often time-varying but not directional. The paper’s pitch is plausible and the multimodal validation story is attractive. The main caution is unchanged by the cleaner framing: effective-connectivity arrows in observational neuroimaging are still not causal identification.
notes.overview: The paper introduces information channel capacity as a model-based measure of directed information transfer between brain regions and couples it with a sliding-window framework to estimate temporal changes in effective connectivity. The validation strategy spans human motor-task functional MRI, concurrent rat local-field-potential plus functional-MRI recordings, and mouse calcium-plus-functional-MRI data. According to the abstract, the method detects stronger task-related directional interactions in human motor regions, shows minimal spurious directional asymmetry relative to scan-to-scan variability in the rat multimodal data, and identifies reproducible connectivity states and transitions in mouse data. The useful read is that this is a potentially intervention-relevant way to characterize network dynamics. The non-useful read would be to confuse directed model output with proven causal mechanism.
notes.whyItMatters: Because intervention logic cares about where activity is going, not only which regions are correlated. Even if the method is still descriptive, it is pointed in a more useful direction than generic dynamic-connectivity maps.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as adjacent methods-side material. It is not enough to ground a therapeutic claim, but it is useful for how to think about dynamic network state estimation.

notes.title: Learning Temporal Basis Vectors for Closed-Loop Neural Stimulation
notes.venue: Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC).
notes.whySelected: It directly targets a real adaptive-stimulation bottleneck by proposing a compact stimulation-response model that is efficient enough to plug into control rather than merely describe data after the fact.
notes.verdictText: This is a preserve note because it aims at the right problem: closed-loop stimulation needs a response model that is sample-efficient, fast to train, and good enough for control. The temporal basis function model looks promising on that front and beats simple linear state-space baselines while staying cheaper than heavier nonlinear dynamical models. The caution is that this is still a conference paper on optogenetic non-human-primate data with simulated closed-loop tests, so it is much more a methods direction than a demonstrated clinical control stack.
notes.overview: The paper introduces a temporal basis function model for forecasting spatiotemporal neural responses to stimulation using recent neural activity and stimulation parameters. The authors position this model as a practical surrogate for closed-loop control methods such as model predictive control or model-based reinforcement learning. They test it on forty micro-electrocorticography sessions from two non-human primates receiving excitatory optogenetic stimulation. According to the abstract, the model needs less than twenty minutes of data collection and about five minutes of training, performs comparably to a more complex nonlinear dynamical model, and outperforms linear state-space baselines like Kalman-filter-style models. They then demonstrate in simulation that the model can steer neural activity toward desired regimes.
notes.whyItMatters: Because adaptive stimulation rhetoric is often much stronger than the modeling stack underneath it. This paper matters precisely because it focuses on the middle layer that many papers skip: a response model simple enough to control, but not so simple that it becomes useless. That is a real path toward less hand-wavy closed-loop neuromodulation.
notes.finalDecision: Keep as a useful computational-control note. Promising, but still early and far from human proof.

notes.title: Implant-Friendly MRI of Deep Brain Stimulation Patients at 3T
notes.whySelected: It tackles an unglamorous but decisive neuroengineering constraint by showing a practical workflow for reducing RF-induced heating and artifact in 3T MRI of DBS patients.
notes.verdictText: This is not a breakthrough targeting paper, but it is worth preserving because platform constraints quietly determine what mechanistic DBS science is possible.
